---
title: C# Types
topic: [Programming]
subtopic: [NET]
summary: "How C# types define shape, behavior, and value versus reference assignment semantics."
tags: [FolderNote]
publish: true
status: Creation
priority: Medium
level: ["4"]
qard-deck: "Programming"
qard-topic: "NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Types"
flashcard_uid: "a5c39ae2"
created: "2026-02-10T16:03:55.000Z"
modified: "2026-11-03T09:57:43.792Z"
published: "2026-07-08T13:14:17.329Z"
---

A C# type defines what values exist, which operations are valid, and what assignment copies. Value types copy their contained value. Reference types copy a reference to one object. That distinction controls aliasing and equality long before stack-versus-heap details matter.

The folder separates the main forms. Classes and record classes are reference types. Structs and record structs are value types. Strings, delegates, and events add specialized behavior on top of the same type system.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Copy and Storage Boundaries

- **Assignment:** a value-type assignment copies every field. Reference fields inside that value still point to the same objects. A reference-type assignment copies the object reference, so both variables can observe mutations to one instance.
- **Arguments:** parameters are passed by value unless marked `ref`, `out`, or `in`. Passing a reference type by value copies the reference, not the object.
- **Storage:** a value type is stored inline in whatever holds it: a local variable, a field of a heap object, or an array element. A reference-type variable holds only a reference to an object instance, so the reference and the object are distinct. Where either physically resides is a runtime detail. Declaration kind therefore does not dictate one physical location.
- **Boxing:** conversion from a value type to `object` or an interface value copies it into a box. Constrained generic calls can often avoid that allocation. Nullable value types box differently: a populated `Nullable<T>` boxes its underlying `T` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating a box.

# Pitfalls

- **Hidden aliases.** Several references can point at one mutable object. Ownership must be clear. Shared models are easier to reason about when immutable.
- **Mutable value copies.** A property, indexer, or `foreach` variable usually exposes a struct copy. Mutation may be rejected by the compiler or affect only the copy. Readonly structs and whole-value replacement keep that boundary visible.
- **Equality chosen by accident.** Classes use reference equality unless they define another contract. Record classes and record structs synthesize value equality, while ordinary structs inherit field-based default equality. Domain identity should decide, not syntax convenience.

# Tradeoffs

- **Class or struct:** a class makes shared identity and inheritance available. A struct gives value-copy semantics and can avoid a separate allocation, but large copies and boxing may cost more.
- **Record class or conventional class:** records fit data whose contents define equality. Identity-rich entities usually need conventional class semantics.
- **Interface or constrained generic:** an interface value gives runtime polymorphism but boxes a struct. A constrained generic can preserve static typing and avoid the box.

# Examples

```csharp
var h = new Holder { Counter = new Counter { Value = 0 } };

// Property access returns a copy of the struct value.
h.Counter.Inc();
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 0

// Fix: replace the whole value after mutation.
var c = h.Counter;
c.Inc();
h.Counter = c;
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 1

public struct Counter
{
    public int Value;
    public void Inc() => Value++;
}

public sealed class Holder
{
    public Counter Counter { get; set; }
}
```

The direct `h.Counter.Inc()` call compiles, but it mutates the temporary value returned by the property and then discards that copy. A direct field assignment such as `h.Counter.Value = 1` is rejected with CS1612. Reading the value into `c`, mutating it, and assigning it back persists the change.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: d8eb59cf-ad2d-43be-954f-44db23f34d38 -->
> [!qard]- Why might mutating a struct inside `foreach` fail to update the collection?
> In an ordinary (non-`ref`) `foreach`, each struct element reaches the loop body as a copy held in a read-only iteration variable. Changes to the copy's own fields never reach the stored element.
>
> - Assigning the iteration variable, or one of its fields, is rejected by the compiler.
> - Calling a mutating method on it compiles, but the method changes the copy's fields rather than the stored element's, so the update is silently lost.
> 
> The copy is shallow. When a field of the struct refers to an object, such as a `List<T>`, the copy and the stored element refer to the same object. A change made to that object through the copy, such as adding an item, therefore remains visible through the collection. Only changes to the struct's own field values are lost.
>
>
> An ordinary struct-valued property has a similar copy boundary: a mutating method call can change only the returned temporary. Direct field assignment through that property may instead be rejected. A property containing a struct enumerator can return a fresh copy on each access, so repeatedly calling MoveNext on the property does not advance one persistent enumerator.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

> [!qard]- How can stored struct elements be updated rather than discarded copies?
> The stored elements can be updated in two ways. The same read-modify-write-back approach applies to an ordinary struct-valued property:
>
> - **Indexed write-back:** a loop by index reads `items[i]` into a local, changes the local and assigns it back to `items[i]`, replacing the whole element value.
> - **`ref` iteration:** when the collection exposes its elements by reference, as `Span<T>` does, `foreach (ref var item in span)` makes `item` an alias for the stored element, so changes apply in place.
> 
> Mutable structs make this mistake easy. Immutable structs, updated by creating a new value and assigning it back, keep the copy boundary visible.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

<!-- qard-id: b89f32ef-f23d-488d-a26a-78ebe0051826 -->
> [!qard]- Where does boxing commonly happen?
> Boxing happens wherever a value type is converted to `object` or to an interface it implements. The runtime allocates an object on the managed heap and copies the value into it. A nullable value type is boxed according to its contents: a populated `int?` boxes its underlying `int` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating.
>
> Common places:
>
> - **`object`-typed variables, collections and parameters:** `object o = 42;`, adding an `int` to a `List<object>` or an `ArrayList`, or passing a struct to a parameter of type `object`.
> - **Interface-typed variables and parameters:** assigning a struct to an `IComparable` variable, or passing it where an interface type is declared.
> 
> Each box is a separate heap allocation that the garbage collector must later reclaim. The box also holds a copy, so later changes to the original value do not affect it.
>
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

> [!qard]- How can boxing be reduced on a measured hot path?
> The conversion to object or an interface value must be removed from the actual call path.
>
> - **Generic collections and APIs:** a generic collection such as `List<int>` is specialized for `int`, so adding an element stores the value without converting it to `object`.
> - **Constrained generics instead of interface-typed parameters:** a method such as `Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>` can call `CompareTo` on a struct argument without converting it to the interface type, provided the struct itself implements that member.
> 
> These changes matter mainly in frequently executed code. They justify extra API complexity where profiling shows boxing allocations are significant.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

<!-- qard-id: d5bda60c-1799-4e4a-ab36-7624ae085e3a -->
> [!qard]- When should a type be a `struct`, `class`, or `record class`?
> The choice follows the semantics the type needs. A `struct` fits a small value that is copied field by field, a `class` fits an object with its own identity, and a `record class` fits a reference type whose contents define its equality. Copying, mutation and measured allocation costs then confirm or adjust that semantic choice.
>
> | Aspect | `struct` | `class` | `record class` |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Assignment and passing | Copies every field, so each variable holds its own field values. The copy is shallow: a reference-type field copies only the reference, so both copies can still point to one object. | Copies a reference, so several variables can share and observe one object. | Copies a reference, as a class does. |
> | Default equality | `Equals` is true when both have the same type and the same stored values. | Equality holds only when both references point to the same object, even if every field matches. | Compiler-generated `Equals` and `==` compare the type and member values. The generated `GetHashCode` compares nothing; it returns hash codes compatible with that equality, so equal records hash equally. |
> | Mutation | A change to a copy's own fields affects only that copy, so such changes are easy to lose. A change to an object reached through a reference field is visible through every copy that shares it. | A change is visible through every reference to the object. | Positional properties are init-only by default, and a `with` expression creates a modified shallow copy whose reference-type members still point to the same objects. |
> | Allocation and cost | Stored inline in the variable, field or array element that holds it, with no allocation of its own. Large values make every copy expensive, and boxing allocates. | One heap allocation per instance. | One heap allocation per instance, as with a class. |
> | Inheritance | Cannot derive from another struct or class or serve as a base type, though it can implement interfaces. | Supports class inheritance. | Can inherit only from another record. |
> | Typical fit | Small data-centric values with little behavior, such as a coordinate. | Entities with identity, a lifecycle or polymorphic behavior. | Data defined by its contents, such as messages or DTOs. |
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) · [Microsoft Learn: Classes (C# language specification)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes) · [Microsoft Learn: Records](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record)

> [!qard]- Why can two anonymous objects compare unequal with `==` but match in `Intersect`?
> Anonymous types synthesize value-based `Equals` and `GetHashCode`, but do not overload `==`; that operator compares reference identity. Two separately created anonymous objects with the same property names, types, order, and values in the same assembly therefore compare unequal with `==` but equal with `Equals`. `Intersect` uses the default equality comparer, which uses their generated equality and hash rather than the `==` operator. Each property is compared with its own type's equality, not recursively by arbitrary object contents. [Microsoft: anonymous types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/anonymous-types)

# References

- [C# type system](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/)

> In an ordinary (non-`ref`) `foreach`, each struct element reaches the loop body as a copy held in a read-only iteration variable. Changes to the copy's own fields never reach the stored element.

> - Assigning the iteration variable, or one of its fields, is rejected by the compiler.

notes.content:
---
title: C# Types
topic: [Programming]
subtopic: [NET]
summary: "How C# types define shape, behavior, and value versus reference assignment semantics."
tags: [FolderNote]
publish: true
status: Creation
priority: Medium
level: ["4"]
qard-deck: "Programming"
qard-topic: "NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Types"
flashcard_uid: "a5c39ae2"
created: "2026-02-10T16:03:55.000Z"
modified: "2026-11-03T09:57:43.792Z"
published: "2026-07-08T13:14:17.329Z"
---

A C# type defines what values exist, which operations are valid, and what assignment copies. Value types copy their contained value. Reference types copy a reference to one object. That distinction controls aliasing and equality long before stack-versus-heap details matter.

The folder separates the main forms. Classes and record classes are reference types. Structs and record structs are value types. Strings, delegates, and events add specialized behavior on top of the same type system.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Copy and Storage Boundaries

- **Assignment:** a value-type assignment copies every field. Reference fields inside that value still point to the same objects. A reference-type assignment copies the object reference, so both variables can observe mutations to one instance.
- **Arguments:** parameters are passed by value unless marked `ref`, `out`, or `in`. Passing a reference type by value copies the reference, not the object.
- **Storage:** a value type is stored inline in whatever holds it: a local variable, a field of a heap object, or an array element. A reference-type variable holds only a reference to an object instance, so the reference and the object are distinct. Where either physically resides is a runtime detail. Declaration kind therefore does not dictate one physical location.
- **Boxing:** conversion from a value type to `object` or an interface value copies it into a box. Constrained generic calls can often avoid that allocation. Nullable value types box differently: a populated `Nullable<T>` boxes its underlying `T` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating a box.

# Pitfalls

- **Hidden aliases.** Several references can point at one mutable object. Ownership must be clear. Shared models are easier to reason about when immutable.
- **Mutable value copies.** A property, indexer, or `foreach` variable usually exposes a struct copy. Mutation may be rejected by the compiler or affect only the copy. Readonly structs and whole-value replacement keep that boundary visible.
- **Equality chosen by accident.** Classes use reference equality unless they define another contract. Record classes and record structs synthesize value equality, while ordinary structs inherit field-based default equality. Domain identity should decide, not syntax convenience.

# Tradeoffs

- **Class or struct:** a class makes shared identity and inheritance available. A struct gives value-copy semantics and can avoid a separate allocation, but large copies and boxing may cost more.
- **Record class or conventional class:** records fit data whose contents define equality. Identity-rich entities usually need conventional class semantics.
- **Interface or constrained generic:** an interface value gives runtime polymorphism but boxes a struct. A constrained generic can preserve static typing and avoid the box.

# Examples

```csharp
var h = new Holder { Counter = new Counter { Value = 0 } };

// Property access returns a copy of the struct value.
h.Counter.Inc();
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 0

// Fix: replace the whole value after mutation.
var c = h.Counter;
c.Inc();
h.Counter = c;
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 1

public struct Counter
{
    public int Value;
    public void Inc() => Value++;
}

public sealed class Holder
{
    public Counter Counter { get; set; }
}
```

The direct `h.Counter.Inc()` call compiles, but it mutates the temporary value returned by the property and then discards that copy. A direct field assignment such as `h.Counter.Value = 1` is rejected with CS1612. Reading the value into `c`, mutating it, and assigning it back persists the change.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: d8eb59cf-ad2d-43be-954f-44db23f34d38 -->
> [!qard]- Why might mutating a struct inside `foreach` fail to update the collection?
> In an ordinary (non-`ref`) `foreach`, each struct element reaches the loop body as a copy held in a read-only iteration variable. Changes to the copy's own fields never reach the stored element.
>
> - Assigning the iteration variable, or one of its fields, is rejected by the compiler.
> - Calling a mutating method on it compiles, but the method changes the copy's fields rather than the stored element's, so the update is silently lost.
> 
> The copy is shallow. When a field of the struct refers to an object, such as a `List<T>`, the copy and the stored element refer to the same object. A change made to that object through the copy, such as adding an item, therefore remains visible through the collection. Only changes to the struct's own field values are lost.
>
>
> An ordinary struct-valued property has a similar copy boundary: a mutating method call can change only the returned temporary. Direct field assignment through that property may instead be rejected. A property containing a struct enumerator can return a fresh copy on each access, so repeatedly calling MoveNext on the property does not advance one persistent enumerator.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

> [!qard]- How can stored struct elements be updated rather than discarded copies?
> The stored elements can be updated in two ways. The same read-modify-write-back approach applies to an ordinary struct-valued property:
>
> - **Indexed write-back:** a loop by index reads `items[i]` into a local, changes the local and assigns it back to `items[i]`, replacing the whole element value.
> - **`ref` iteration:** when the collection exposes its elements by reference, as `Span<T>` does, `foreach (ref var item in span)` makes `item` an alias for the stored element, so changes apply in place.
> 
> Mutable structs make this mistake easy. Immutable structs, updated by creating a new value and assigning it back, keep the copy boundary visible.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

<!-- qard-id: b89f32ef-f23d-488d-a26a-78ebe0051826 -->
> [!qard]- Where does boxing commonly happen?
> Boxing happens wherever a value type is converted to `object` or to an interface it implements. The runtime allocates an object on the managed heap and copies the value into it. A nullable value type is boxed according to its contents: a populated `int?` boxes its underlying `int` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating.
>
> Common places:
>
> - **`object`-typed variables, collections and parameters:** `object o = 42;`, adding an `int` to a `List<object>` or an `ArrayList`, or passing a struct to a parameter of type `object`.
> - **Interface-typed variables and parameters:** assigning a struct to an `IComparable` variable, or passing it where an interface type is declared.
> 
> Each box is a separate heap allocation that the garbage collector must later reclaim. The box also holds a copy, so later changes to the original value do not affect it.
>
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

> [!qard]- How can boxing be reduced on a measured hot path?
> The conversion to object or an interface value must be removed from the actual call path.
>
> - **Generic collections and APIs:** a generic collection such as `List<int>` is specialized for `int`, so adding an element stores the value without converting it to `object`.
> - **Constrained generics instead of interface-typed parameters:** a method such as `Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>` can call `CompareTo` on a struct argument without converting it to the interface type, provided the struct itself implements that member.
> 
> These changes matter mainly in frequently executed code. They justify extra API complexity where profiling shows boxing allocations are significant.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

<!-- qard-id: d5bda60c-1799-4e4a-ab36-7624ae085e3a -->
> [!qard]- When should a type be a `struct`, `class`, or `record class`?
> The choice follows the semantics the type needs. A `struct` fits a small value that is copied field by field, a `class` fits an object with its own identity, and a `record class` fits a reference type whose contents define its equality. Copying, mutation and measured allocation costs then confirm or adjust that semantic choice.
>
> | Aspect | `struct` | `class` | `record class` |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Assignment and passing | Copies every field, so each variable holds its own field values. The copy is shallow: a reference-type field copies only the reference, so both copies can still point to one object. | Copies a reference, so several variables can share and observe one object. | Copies a reference, as a class does. |
> | Default equality | `Equals` is true when both have the same type and the same stored values. | Equality holds only when both references point to the same object, even if every field matches. | Compiler-generated `Equals` and `==` compare the type and member values. The generated `GetHashCode` compares nothing; it returns hash codes compatible with that equality, so equal records hash equally. |
> | Mutation | A change to a copy's own fields affects only that copy, so such changes are easy to lose. A change to an object reached through a reference field is visible through every copy that shares it. | A change is visible through every reference to the object. | Positional properties are init-only by default, and a `with` expression creates a modified shallow copy whose reference-type members still point to the same objects. |
> | Allocation and cost | Stored inline in the variable, field or array element that holds it, with no allocation of its own. Large values make every copy expensive, and boxing allocates. | One heap allocation per instance. | One heap allocation per instance, as with a class. |
> | Inheritance | Cannot derive from another struct or class or serve as a base type, though it can implement interfaces. | Supports class inheritance. | Can inherit only from another record. |
> | Typical fit | Small data-centric values with little behavior, such as a coordinate. | Entities with identity, a lifecycle or polymorphic behavior. | Data defined by its contents, such as messages or DTOs. |
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) · [Microsoft Learn: Classes (C# language specification)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes) · [Microsoft Learn: Records](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record)

> [!qard]- Why can two anonymous objects compare unequal with `==` but match in `Intersect`?
> Anonymous types synthesize value-based `Equals` and `GetHashCode`, but do not overload `==`; that operator compares reference identity. Two separately created anonymous objects with the same property names, types, order, and values in the same assembly therefore compare unequal with `==` but equal with `Equals`. `Intersect` uses the default equality comparer, which uses their generated equality and hash rather than the `==` operator. Each property is compared with its own type's equality, not recursively by arbitrary object contents. [Microsoft: anonymous types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/anonymous-types)

# References

- [C# type system](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/)

summary: "The default in-process mutual-exclusion primitive: one thread in the critical section at a time."

`lock` gives one thread at a time access to a synchronous critical section. It fits small in-process state changes such as updating a counter or taking a snapshot of a shared dictionary. Awaited I/O should normally happen outside that mutation and publish its result inside a short lock. When an invariant genuinely must span asynchronous work, `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync` can gate that bounded span; cross-process coordination needs [[Mutex]], and N concurrent holders need [[Semaphore]] rather than mutual exclusion.

# How It Works

`lock (obj) { body }` is sugar over `Monitor`:

```csharp
lock (_gate) { _count++; }

// the compiler emits:
bool lockTaken = false;
try
{
    Monitor.Enter(_gate, ref lockTaken);
    _count++;
}
finally
{
    if (lockTaken) Monitor.Exit(_gate);
}
```

`lockTaken` records whether `Monitor.Enter` succeeded. If acquisition throws, the `finally` block does not attempt to release a monitor the thread never owned.

**`Monitor`/`lock` is reentrant.** Its owning thread can acquire the same monitor again. Each acquisition increments a recursion count, so the thread must exit the same number of times. A one-permit [[Semaphore|semaphore]] has no such ownership model and self-deadlocks on a nested wait.

**`System.Threading.Lock` (.NET 9+)** makes this intent explicit. When the operand has type `Lock`, the statement uses `Lock.EnterScope()` and disposes its `ref struct` scope at the closing brace instead of lowering to `Monitor.Enter`:

```csharp
private readonly Lock _gate = new();   // .NET 9+

lock (_gate) { _count++; }             // compiler calls _gate.EnterScope()
```

A dedicated `Lock` field is harder to misuse than a general `object`. With either type, the gate stays `private readonly`. Locking on `this`, a `Type`, or an interned string exposes the monitor to unrelated code and can create invisible [[Deadlocks|lock-ordering cycles]].

# Example

```csharp
public sealed class MetricsBuffer
{
    private readonly Lock _gate = new();          // .NET 9+; an `object` pre-9
    private readonly Dictionary<string, long> _counts = new();

    public void Increment(string name)
    {
        lock (_gate)
        {
            _counts.TryGetValue(name, out long n);
            _counts[name] = n + 1;
        }
    }

    public IReadOnlyDictionary<string, long> Snapshot()
    {
        lock (_gate)
            return new Dictionary<string, long>(_counts);  // copy out under the lock
    }
}
```

Both reads and writes use `_gate`. `Snapshot` copies the dictionary while protected, then returns data that callers can enumerate after the live lock has been released.

# Pitfalls

- **A monitor cannot span `await`.** Monitor ownership has thread affinity, while a continuation may resume on another thread. The compiler reports CS1996. Async mutual exclusion uses a [[Semaphore|semaphore]] and `WaitAsync`.
- **I/O inside a lock turns latency into contention.** Every waiter queues behind the slow operation, increasing the chance of convoys and [[Deadlocks|deadlocks]]. Computation and fetching belong outside the lock, which then protects only the shared-state update.
- **A public gate leaks synchronization.** `this`, a `Type`, and interned strings can all be locked by unrelated code.
- **`Monitor.TryEnter(obj, timeout)` bounds acquisition.** It is useful when an external lock order cannot be fully controlled. [[Deadlocks]] covers the ordering mechanics.

# Tradeoffs

- **`lock`/`Monitor`** is synchronous, in-process, reentrant mutual exclusion. Its fast path stays in user mode.
- **`SemaphoreSlim`** is in-process, supports `WaitAsync`, and can expose more than one permit. It has no thread ownership or reentrancy.
- **`Mutex`** supplies thread-owned mutual exclusion through an operating-system object and can coordinate named participants across processes.

For short synchronous state changes inside one process, `lock` is the smallest correct primitive. Ordinary async flows need restructuring so awaited I/O completes before the protected mutation. When the invariant must remain gated across asynchronous work, `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync` provides that gate, and the span needs to stay bounded because remote latency becomes contention. A real process boundary justifies `Mutex`. N concurrent entrants make the problem a [[Semaphore]] problem regardless of whether callers wait synchronously or asynchronously.

# Questions

> [!qard]- What is a race condition?
> A race condition occurs when a result depends on the timing of concurrent accesses to shared state. A read-modify-write sequence such as `_count++` can let two threads read the same old value, then overwrite one another's updates. A run that happens to produce the expected result does not prove the code is race-free.
>
> [Microsoft: Managed threading best practices](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/managed-threading-best-practices) · [Microsoft: `lock` statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock)

> [!qard]- How does `lock` prevent a lost-update race?
> `lock` lets only one thread at a time run code protected by the same lock object, so protected updates cannot interleave.
>
> For example, two threads run `_count++` on a shared field. The increment is three steps: read the value, add one and write the result back.
>
> 1. Thread A reads 5.
> 2. Thread B reads 5 before A writes.
> 3. A writes 6.
> 4. B writes 6.
> 
> Two increments ran, but one was lost. With `lock (_gate) { _count++; }` in both threads, B cannot read until A has written and released the lock, so the result is 7.
>
> The protection covers only code that takes the same lock. Every read and write of the shared state must use that lock object; an unprotected access elsewhere can still interleave with a protected update.
>
> [Microsoft: Managed threading best practices](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/managed-threading-best-practices) · [Microsoft: `lock` statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock)

<!-- qard-id: e403b36e-6e7b-4f41-826c-e2e258743019 -->
> [!qard]- When `lock` targets an ordinary object, what does the compiler ensure around the critical section?
> The compiler acquires the monitor with `Monitor.Enter(obj, ref lockTaken)`, runs the body inside `try`, and exits in `finally` only if acquisition succeeded. This releases ownership on normal and exceptional exits without exiting a monitor the thread never acquired. The specialized `System.Threading.Lock` path in C# 13 uses `EnterScope` instead. [Microsoft: `lock` statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock) · [Monitor.Enter](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.monitor.enter?view=net-10.0)

<!-- qard-id: 2c0335e4-1efa-4aa3-b33b-605b74456ccc -->
> [!qard]- Why can’t a `lock` block contain `await`?
> `Monitor` ownership belongs to the thread that entered it, and only that thread can exit it. An awaited continuation may resume on a different thread, which would then try to release a monitor it does not own. The C# compiler therefore rejects `await` inside a `lock` block.
>
> Holding a lock across `await` would also make other threads wait for the whole asynchronous operation, turning I/O latency into lock contention.
>
> Two alternatives remain:
>
> - **Restructure:** the awaited work runs outside the lock, and only the resulting state change runs inside a short `lock`. This fits most cases.
> - **Async-aware gate:** when an invariant must stay protected across an `await`, a `SemaphoreSlim` with one permit and `await WaitAsync()` provides the gate. It has no thread ownership, so a continuation on another thread can release it. `Release()` belongs in `finally`.
> 
> [Microsoft: `lock` statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock) · [Monitor.Enter](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.monitor.enter?view=net-10.0) · [SemaphoreSlim API](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0)

<!-- qard-id: 9e14d6f6-6dc4-4b82-bda7-880929057d58 -->
> [!qard]- What does `System.Threading.Lock` change about `lock` in C# 13 and .NET 9+?
> `System.Threading.Lock` gives the compiler a dedicated synchronization type instead of an arbitrary object. In C# 13, `lock` on that type lowers to an `EnterScope()` guard that releases when the scope exits, rather than the ordinary `Monitor.Enter`/`Exit` pattern. It remains synchronous and cannot span `await`; the type does not promise a universal speedup. [Microsoft: `lock` statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock)

<!-- qard-id: 0fdc576b-ea0a-41ce-9613-4ec6f7fe0d57 -->
> [!qard]- How does reentrancy differ between `lock`/`Monitor` and `SemaphoreSlim`?
> `lock`/`Monitor` is reentrant for its owning thread. `SemaphoreSlim` is not reentrant, because it has no owner.
>
> - **`lock`/`Monitor`:** records which thread owns the monitor and how many times it has entered. The owner can enter again without blocking, and other threads can acquire the monitor only after the owner has exited the same number of times.
> - **`SemaphoreSlim`:** records only how many permits remain, not which thread or asynchronous flow holds them. A second wait from the same code is just another request for a permit.
> 
> With a one-permit `SemaphoreSlim`, a method that holds the permit and then calls code that waits on the same semaphore ends up waiting for itself. Without a timeout or cancellation, `Wait()` blocks forever and `WaitAsync()` never completes. The permit therefore belongs at one boundary in the call chain, with `Release()` in `finally` so that each acquisition is released exactly once.
>
> [Microsoft: `lock` statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock) · [Monitor.Enter](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.monitor.enter?view=net-10.0) · [SemaphoreSlim API](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0)

> [!qard]- When is `Interlocked` sufficient instead of `lock`?
> `Interlocked` fits a supported atomic update to one shared location, such as incrementing a counter or exchanging a reference. Its read-modify-write operation cannot lose an update through interleaving:
>
> ```csharp
> Interlocked.Increment(ref completedCount);
> ```
>
> That one atomic operation does not make a sequence of operations or several related fields atomic. A check-then-update rule or a multi-field invariant needs a suitable synchronization design, often one lock around the entire decision and change. In a worker-count example, waiting for every worker to finish is also necessary before asserting the final count. [Microsoft: Interlocked](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.interlocked?view=net-10.0)

---

modified: "2026-11-03T09:57:43.792Z"

---

A C# type defines what values exist, which operations are valid, and what assignment copies. Value types copy their contained value. Reference types copy a reference to one object. That distinction controls aliasing and equality long before stack-versus-heap details matter.

The folder separates the main forms. Classes and record classes are reference types. Structs and record structs are value types. Strings, delegates, and events add specialized behavior on top of the same type system.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Copy and Storage Boundaries

- **Assignment:** a value-type assignment copies every field. Reference fields inside that value still point to the same objects. A reference-type assignment copies the object reference, so both variables can observe mutations to one instance.
- **Arguments:** parameters are passed by value unless marked `ref`, `out`, or `in`. Passing a reference type by value copies the reference, not the object.
- **Storage:** a value type is stored inline in whatever holds it: a local variable, a field of a heap object, or an array element. A reference-type variable holds only a reference to an object instance, so the reference and the object are distinct. Where either physically resides is a runtime detail. Declaration kind therefore does not dictate one physical location.
- **Boxing:** conversion from a value type to `object` or an interface value copies it into a box. Constrained generic calls can often avoid that allocation. Nullable value types box differently: a populated `Nullable<T>` boxes its underlying `T` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating a box.

# Pitfalls

- **Hidden aliases.** Several references can point at one mutable object. Ownership must be clear. Shared models are easier to reason about when immutable.
- **Mutable value copies.** A property, indexer, or `foreach` variable usually exposes a struct copy. Mutation may be rejected by the compiler or affect only the copy. Readonly structs and whole-value replacement keep that boundary visible.
- **Equality chosen by accident.** Classes use reference equality unless they define another contract. Record classes and record structs synthesize value equality, while ordinary structs inherit field-based default equality. Domain identity should decide, not syntax convenience.

# Tradeoffs

- **Class or struct:** a class makes shared identity and inheritance available. A struct gives value-copy semantics and can avoid a separate allocation, but large copies and boxing may cost more.
- **Record class or conventional class:** records fit data whose contents define equality. Identity-rich entities usually need conventional class semantics.
- **Interface or constrained generic:** an interface value gives runtime polymorphism but boxes a struct. A constrained generic can preserve static typing and avoid the box.

# Examples

```csharp
var h = new Holder { Counter = new Counter { Value = 0 } };

// Property access returns a copy of the struct value.
h.Counter.Inc();
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 0

// Fix: replace the whole value after mutation.
var c = h.Counter;
c.Inc();
h.Counter = c;
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 1

public struct Counter
{
    public int Value;
    public void Inc() => Value++;
}

public sealed class Holder
{
    public Counter Counter { get; set; }
}
```

The direct `h.Counter.Inc()` call compiles, but it mutates the temporary value returned by the property and then discards that copy. A direct field assignment such as `h.Counter.Value = 1` is rejected with CS1612. Reading the value into `c`, mutating it, and assigning it back persists the change.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: d8eb59cf-ad2d-43be-954f-44db23f34d38 -->
> [!qard]- Why might mutating a struct inside `foreach` fail to update the collection?
> In an ordinary (non-`ref`) `foreach`, each struct element reaches the loop body as a copy held in a read-only iteration variable. Changes to the copy's own fields never reach the stored element.
>
> - Assigning the iteration variable, or one of its fields, is rejected by the compiler.
> - Calling a mutating method on it compiles, but the method changes the copy's fields rather than the stored element's, so the update is silently lost.
> 
> The copy is shallow. When a field of the struct refers to an object, such as a `List<T>`, the copy and the stored element refer to the same object. A change made to that object through the copy, such as adding an item, therefore remains visible through the collection. Only changes to the struct's own field values are lost.
>
>
> An ordinary struct-valued property has a similar copy boundary: a mutating method call can change only the returned temporary. Direct field assignment through that property may instead be rejected. A property containing a struct enumerator can return a fresh copy on each access, so repeatedly calling MoveNext on the property does not advance one persistent enumerator.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

> [!qard]- How can stored struct elements be updated rather than discarded copies?
> The stored elements can be updated in two ways. The same read-modify-write-back approach applies to an ordinary struct-valued property:
>
> - **Indexed write-back:** a loop by index reads `items[i]` into a local, changes the local and assigns it back to `items[i]`, replacing the whole element value.
> - **`ref` iteration:** when the collection exposes its elements by reference, as `Span<T>` does, `foreach (ref var item in span)` makes `item` an alias for the stored element, so changes apply in place.
> 
> Mutable structs make this mistake easy. Immutable structs, updated by creating a new value and assigning it back, keep the copy boundary visible.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

<!-- qard-id: b89f32ef-f23d-488d-a26a-78ebe0051826 -->
> [!qard]- Where does boxing commonly happen?
> Boxing happens wherever a value type is converted to `object` or to an interface it implements. The runtime allocates an object on the managed heap and copies the value into it. A nullable value type is boxed according to its contents: a populated `int?` boxes its underlying `int` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating.
>
> Common places:
>
> - **`object`-typed variables, collections and parameters:** `object o = 42;`, adding an `int` to a `List<object>` or an `ArrayList`, or passing a struct to a parameter of type `object`.
> - **Interface-typed variables and parameters:** assigning a struct to an `IComparable` variable, or passing it where an interface type is declared.
> 
> Each box is a separate heap allocation that the garbage collector must later reclaim. The box also holds a copy, so later changes to the original value do not affect it.
>
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

> [!qard]- How can boxing be reduced on a measured hot path?
> The conversion to object or an interface value must be removed from the actual call path.
>
> - **Generic collections and APIs:** a generic collection such as `List<int>` is specialized for `int`, so adding an element stores the value without converting it to `object`.
> - **Constrained generics instead of interface-typed parameters:** a method such as `Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>` can call `CompareTo` on a struct argument without converting it to the interface type, provided the struct itself implements that member.
> 
> These changes matter mainly in frequently executed code. They justify extra API complexity where profiling shows boxing allocations are significant.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

<!-- qard-id: d5bda60c-1799-4e4a-ab36-7624ae085e3a -->
> [!qard]- When should a type be a `struct`, `class`, or `record class`?
> The choice follows the semantics the type needs. A `struct` fits a small value that is copied field by field, a `class` fits an object with its own identity, and a `record class` fits a reference type whose contents define its equality. Copying, mutation and measured allocation costs then confirm or adjust that semantic choice.
>
> | Aspect | `struct` | `class` | `record class` |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Assignment and passing | Copies every field, so each variable holds its own field values. The copy is shallow: a reference-type field copies only the reference, so both copies can still point to one object. | Copies a reference, so several variables can share and observe one object. | Copies a reference, as a class does. |
> | Default equality | `Equals` is true when both have the same type and the same stored values. | Equality holds only when both references point to the same object, even if every field matches. | Compiler-generated `Equals` and `==` compare the type and member values. The generated `GetHashCode` compares nothing; it returns hash codes compatible with that equality, so equal records hash equally. |
> | Mutation | A change to a copy's own fields affects only that copy, so such changes are easy to lose. A change to an object reached through a reference field is visible through every copy that shares it. | A change is visible through every reference to the object. | Positional properties are init-only by default, and a `with` expression creates a modified shallow copy whose reference-type members still point to the same objects. |
> | Allocation and cost | Stored inline in the variable, field or array element that holds it, with no allocation of its own. Large values make every copy expensive, and boxing allocates. | One heap allocation per instance. | One heap allocation per instance, as with a class. |
> | Inheritance | Cannot derive from another struct or class or serve as a base type, though it can implement interfaces. | Supports class inheritance. | Can inherit only from another record. |
> | Typical fit | Small data-centric values with little behavior, such as a coordinate. | Entities with identity, a lifecycle or polymorphic behavior. | Data defined by its contents, such as messages or DTOs. |
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) · [Microsoft Learn: Classes (C# language specification)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes) · [Microsoft Learn: Records](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record)

> [!qard]- Why can two anonymous objects compare unequal with `==` but match in `Intersect`?
> Anonymous types synthesize value-based `Equals` and `GetHashCode`, but do not overload `==`; that operator compares reference identity. Two separately created anonymous objects with the same property names, types, order, and values in the same assembly therefore compare unequal with `==` but equal with `Equals`. `Intersect` uses the default equality comparer, which uses their generated equality and hash rather than the `==` operator. Each property is compared with its own type's equality, not recursively by arbitrary object contents. [Microsoft: anonymous types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/anonymous-types)

# References

- [C# type system](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/)

notes.content:
---
topic: [AI & ML]
subtopic: [LLM]
summary: "Mapping text into a dense vector space where semantic similarity becomes geometric proximity."
level: ["2"]
priority: High
status: Done
publish: true
qard-deck: "AI & ML"
qard-topic: "LLM/Embeddings"
flashcard_uid: "485a25d5"
created: "2026-02-27T12:56:16.000Z"
modified: "2026-11-02T09:03:54.806Z"
published: "2026-07-08T13:28:37.406Z"
---

Embeddings turn text into vectors so that related meanings occupy nearby points. That geometry lets retrieval match "throttle partner API traffic" with a document about "rate limiting for partner plan" even when the wording does not overlap.

An encoder model, usually a transformer trained with a contrastive objective, reads a text span and produces a fixed-length vector. Training pulls similar pairs together and pushes unrelated pairs apart. At query time, the same model embeds the query, and the index finds nearby stored vectors with cosine similarity or dot product. Those neighbors are the candidate chunks.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Q as Query Text
    participant E as Embedding Model
    participant VS as Vector Space
    participant I as ANN Index
    participant R as Top-k Results
    Q->>E: Encode query
    E->>VS: Query vector 1x768
    Note over VS: Cosine similarity\nagainst stored chunk vectors
    VS->>I: ANN search -- HNSW or IVF
    I->>R: Return k nearest chunks
```

Leaderboard quality is only a starting point. The useful model is the one that meets recall and latency targets on the actual corpus, at an acceptable cost. A model that tops MTEB can still mishandle internal terminology.

# Embedding Model Selection

## Model Families

Production RAG systems usually start with one of these model families.

**Proprietary API models.** OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` (1536 dimensions) and `text-embedding-3-large` (3072 dimensions) support a `dimensions` parameter for Matryoshka truncation at inference time. Cohere `embed-v3` distinguishes `search_document` from `search_query` through `input_type` and covers more than 100 languages. Per-token rates change, so cost comparisons need current provider pricing.

**Open-source bi-encoders.** Sentence Transformers (SBERT) includes `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (384 dimensions, 22M parameters) and `all-mpnet-base-v2` (768 dimensions, 109M parameters). Local inference removes per-token API charges, but the serving hardware and model lifecycle become an internal concern.

**Domain-finetuned models.** A base model can be adapted when internal terminology is the measured source of retrieval misses. In a Databricks FinanceBench experiment, `gte-large-en-v1.5` (0.4B parameters) fine-tuned on synthetic domain data reached [[Monitoring#Retrieval Quality Metrics|Recall@10]] of 0.552 versus 0.44 for `text-embedding-3-large`. Adaptation commonly uses continued masked-language pre-training or contrastive training on query-document pairs.

## Dimensionality

Higher dimensions give the model more room to represent fine-grained distinctions. But higher dimensions also mean more storage (4 bytes × dimensions per vector), more compute for similarity search, and higher ANN index memory.

Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) trains models so that prefixes of the full vector remain independently meaningful. OpenAI reports `text-embedding-3-large` at 256 dimensions outperforming `ada-002` at 1536 dimensions on the aggregate MTEB benchmark. That result motivates testing shorter vectors, but corpus-specific Recall@k must establish the retrieval tradeoff. Shorter vectors can reduce storage and search work, with full dimensions reserved for cases that need them.

A two-stage design can generate the full embedding once, normalize and index its reduced prefix for ANN search, then score the small candidate set with the retained full vector or a cross-encoder. Full vectors must live outside the ANN index or be recomputed for the candidates. Retaining them reduces ANN memory and search work but not total vector storage; recomputing them trades storage for API cost and latency.

## Similarity Metrics

The similarity metric defines what "near" means in the vector space.

**Cosine similarity** measures the angle between vectors, ignoring magnitude. Most embedding models are trained with cosine objectives, making it the default choice. Range: -1 to 1 (1 = identical direction).

**Dot product** is cosine similarity scaled by vector magnitudes. For L2-normalized vectors, dot product equals cosine similarity. Normalization is model-specific: OpenAI documents its embedding vectors as length-normalized, while another model may preserve magnitude as part of the signal. The selected model's documentation, not a general assumption about every API, determines whether its vectors are normalized.

**Euclidean (L2) distance** measures straight-line distance in vector space. For length-normalized vectors, squared L2 distance equals 2 − 2 × cosine similarity, so L2 and cosine produce identical rankings; OpenAI documents this for its normalized embeddings. For unnormalized vectors, L2 also reflects vector magnitude and can rank neighbors differently from cosine, so the metric follows the geometry the model's documentation specifies.

Cosine similarity is the safe default unless the model documentation specifies another metric.

# Pitfalls

## Distribution Shift on Internal Terminology

A model that scores well on MTEB can still fail on a specific domain. Internal acronyms or product names may be poorly represented in the training data, leaving related queries and documents far apart in vector space.

Detection: recall@k on a held-out set of domain-specific queries is compared with recall@k on generic queries. A significant gap signals distribution shift.

The repair depends on the failure. Domain adaptation can improve semantic placement, while [[Retrieval|hybrid retrieval]] lets BM25 recover exact terminology that dense retrieval misses.

## Embedding Model Swap Invalidation

Changing the embedding model — even a minor version — invalidates every stored vector. The new model produces vectors in a different geometric space. Cosine similarity between old and new vectors is meaningless.

This means re-embedding the entire corpus: for a 10M-chunk index at $0.02/1M tokens and 500 tokens/chunk average, that is ~$100 and hours of ingestion time. Keying the [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/RAG Caching|embedding cache]] by model name + version prevents serving stale vectors.

## Benchmark Leaderboard Overfitting

MTEB aggregates several task families. A model can rank first overall while performing poorly on retrieval because strong classification or semantic-similarity results lift its average. RAG selection therefore uses the `Retrieval` category scores and then a test against a corpus-specific evaluation set.

## Multilingual Embedding Collapse

Models trained primarily on English text cluster non-English content into a smaller region of vector space, reducing separation between distinct concepts. A Spanish query about "seguridad informática" and one about "seguridad alimentaria" may land closer together than they should because the model undertrained on Spanish semantic distinctions.

Mitigation: models with explicit multilingual training (Cohere `embed-v3`, SBERT multilingual variants) reduce the risk, and recall is evaluated per language separately.

# Tradeoffs

| Factor | Proprietary API | Open-Source Self-Hosted | Domain-Finetuned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost at scale | Per-token pricing -- scales linearly | Infrastructure cost -- GPU amortized across volume | Training cost upfront -- inference same as base |
| Recall on general text | High -- trained on massive web corpora | Competitive -- top models match proprietary on MTEB | Depends on base model and training data quality |
| Recall on domain text | Can miss internal terminology | Same limitation as proprietary | Potentially higher when domain training improves held-out retrieval |
| Latency | Network round-trip + provider queue | Local inference -- no network hop | Same as self-hosted base model |
| Operational burden | Minimal -- API call | High -- GPU infra and model serving and updates | Highest -- training pipeline plus serving |
| Vendor lock-in | Model changes break vector index | Full control over versioning | Full control |
| Dimensionality control | Some models support MRL truncation | Full control via model choice | Full control |

The simplest model that establishes a credible recall baseline is the right starting point. Fine-tuning is justified only after failed queries show that domain semantics, rather than chunk boundaries or retrieval configuration, are the bottleneck. Better embeddings cannot repair bad chunks.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: bb5874a0-b6ba-4318-ab29-25a6079c807a -->
> [!qard]- How do embeddings support semantic retrieval?
> An embedding is a vector of numbers that a model produces for a piece of text. The model places texts with related meaning close together, so the distance between two vectors measures how related the texts are. The vector's length is set by the model and, for some models such as OpenAI's `text-embedding-3` family, by a requested output size.
>
> Semantic retrieval relies on that geometry:
>
> 1. **Indexing:** the embedding model converts each document chunk into a vector, which is stored in a vector index.
> 2. **Query:** the same model, with the same output size, converts the query into a vector in the same space.
> 3. **Ranking:** a similarity measure, such as cosine similarity, ranks the stored vectors by closeness to the query vector. The nearest chunks become retrieval candidates.
>
> Because matching depends on meaning rather than shared words, a query about throttling partner API traffic can find a document about rate limiting for partners. A high similarity score is only a relevance signal. It does not prove that a chunk answers the question, so retrieval quality still has to be evaluated.
>
> [Vector embeddings (OpenAI)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings) · [Vector search overview (Azure AI Search)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview)

<!-- qard-id: cbeb031d-1919-44df-9d70-3df6fafd8901 -->
> [!qard]- How do Matryoshka embeddings reduce vector storage?
> Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) trains an embedding so that its first dimensions already form a useful coarse representation, and later dimensions add finer detail. A prefix of the vector, such as its first 256 values, therefore still works as a lower-dimensional embedding. Storing only that prefix reduces vector storage.
>
> - **Storage:** at the same data type, 256 values instead of 1536 is one-sixth of the raw vector payload. IDs, metadata and index structures do not shrink by the same factor, so the whole index shrinks less.
> - **Search cost:** shorter vectors also reduce distance-computation work.
> - **Availability:** shortening is model-specific. OpenAI's `text-embedding-3` models accept a `dimensions` parameter. A vector truncated manually is re-normalized before cosine or dot-product search.
>
> [Embeddings guide (OpenAI)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings) · [Matryoshka Representation Learning (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13147)

> [!qard]- How should a shorter embedding dimension be validated?
> Fewer embedding dimensions can lower retrieval quality on a particular corpus.
>
> A shorter vector is validated by running the same labeled queries at each candidate dimension and comparing Recall@k and latency. The preferred dimension is the smallest one that still meets the recall and latency targets. A design that re-scores candidates with full-length vectors has to store them elsewhere or recompute them, which adds storage, API cost or latency.
>
> [Embeddings guide (OpenAI)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings) · [Matryoshka Representation Learning (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13147)

<!-- qard-id: d153db49-a943-4334-bb4e-310ba8915adb -->
> [!qard]- What happens to retrieval when queries use embeddings from a new model but the corpus still has vectors from the old model?
> Retrieval quality breaks. The query vector and the stored vectors come from different vector spaces, so the distances between them do not measure relatedness, and the ranking becomes effectively arbitrary.
>
> Each embedding model learns its own coordinate system, so the same text receives unrelated vectors from two different models. If both models produce vectors of the same length, the search can still run without any error while returning poor results. That makes the mismatch easy to miss.
>
> A model change therefore requires re-embedding the whole corpus with the new model. A safe migration builds and validates the new index first and only then switches query traffic, for example by moving a collection alias. Embedding-cache keys include the model name and version, so cached vectors from the old model are not reused with the new one.
>
> [Configure a vectorizer (Azure AI Search)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-configure-vectorizer)

MTEB aggregates several task families. A model can rank first overall while performing poorly on retrieval because strong classification or semantic-similarity results lift its average. RAG selection therefore uses the `Retrieval` category scores and then a test against a corpus-specific evaluation set.

## Multilingual Embedding Collapse

Models trained primarily on English text cluster non-English content into a smaller region of vector space, reducing separation between distinct concepts. A Spanish query about "seguridad informática" and one about "seguridad alimentaria" may land closer together than they should because the model undertrained on Spanish semantic distinctions.

| Factor | Proprietary API | Open-Source Self-Hosted | Domain-Finetuned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost at scale | Per-token pricing -- scales linearly | Infrastructure cost -- GPU amortized across volume | Training cost upfront -- inference same as base |

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: bb5874a0-b6ba-4318-ab29-25a6079c807a -->
> [!qard]- How do embeddings support semantic retrieval?
> An embedding is a vector of numbers that a model produces for a piece of text. The model places texts with related meaning close together, so the distance between two vectors measures how related the texts are. The vector's length is set by the model and, for some models such as OpenAI's `text-embedding-3` family, by a requested output size.

>

> 2. **Query:** the same model, with the same output size, converts the query into a vector in the same space.

<!-- qard-id: cbeb031d-1919-44df-9d70-3df6fafd8901 -->
> [!qard]- How do Matryoshka embeddings reduce vector storage?

> [!qard]- How should a shorter embedding dimension be validated?

>

> [Embeddings guide (OpenAI)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings) · [Matryoshka Representation Learning (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13147)

<!-- qard-id: d153db49-a943-4334-bb4e-310ba8915adb -->
> [!qard]- What happens to retrieval when queries use embeddings from a new model but the corpus still has vectors from the old model?

>
> [Configure a vectorizer (Azure AI Search)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-configure-vectorizer)

Embeddings turn text into vectors so that related meanings occupy nearby points. That geometry lets retrieval match "throttle partner API traffic" with a document about "rate limiting for partner plan" even when the wording does not overlap.

An encoder model, usually a transformer trained with a contrastive objective, reads a text span and produces a fixed-length vector. Training pulls similar pairs together and pushes unrelated pairs apart. At query time, the same model embeds the query, and the index finds nearby stored vectors with cosine similarity or dot product. Those neighbors are the candidate chunks.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Q as Query Text
    participant E as Embedding Model
    participant VS as Vector Space
    participant I as ANN Index
    participant R as Top-k Results
    Q->>E: Encode query
    E->>VS: Query vector 1x768
    Note over VS: Cosine similarity\nagainst stored chunk vectors
    VS->>I: ANN search -- HNSW or IVF
    I->>R: Return k nearest chunks
```

Leaderboard quality is only a starting point. The useful model is the one that meets recall and latency targets on the actual corpus, at an acceptable cost. A model that tops MTEB can still mishandle internal terminology.

# Embedding Model Selection

## Model Families

Production RAG systems usually start with one of these model families.

**Proprietary API models.** OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` (1536 dimensions) and `text-embedding-3-large` (3072 dimensions) support a `dimensions` parameter for Matryoshka truncation at inference time. Cohere `embed-v3` distinguishes `search_document` from `search_query` through `input_type` and covers more than 100 languages. Per-token rates change, so cost comparisons need current provider pricing.

**Open-source bi-encoders.** Sentence Transformers (SBERT) includes `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (384 dimensions, 22M parameters) and `all-mpnet-base-v2` (768 dimensions, 109M parameters). Local inference removes per-token API charges, but the serving hardware and model lifecycle become an internal concern.

**Domain-finetuned models.** A base model can be adapted when internal terminology is the measured source of retrieval misses. In a Databricks FinanceBench experiment, `gte-large-en-v1.5` (0.4B parameters) fine-tuned on synthetic domain data reached [[Monitoring#Retrieval Quality Metrics|Recall@10]] of 0.552 versus 0.44 for `text-embedding-3-large`. Adaptation commonly uses continued masked-language pre-training or contrastive training on query-document pairs.

## Dimensionality

Higher dimensions give the model more room to represent fine-grained distinctions. But higher dimensions also mean more storage (4 bytes × dimensions per vector), more compute for similarity search, and higher ANN index memory.

Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) trains models so that prefixes of the full vector remain independently meaningful. OpenAI reports `text-embedding-3-large` at 256 dimensions outperforming `ada-002` at 1536 dimensions on the aggregate MTEB benchmark. That result motivates testing shorter vectors, but corpus-specific Recall@k must establish the retrieval tradeoff. Shorter vectors can reduce storage and search work, with full dimensions reserved for cases that need them.

A two-stage design can generate the full embedding once, normalize and index its reduced prefix for ANN search, then score the small candidate set with the retained full vector or a cross-encoder. Full vectors must live outside the ANN index or be recomputed for the candidates. Retaining them reduces ANN memory and search work but not total vector storage; recomputing them trades storage for API cost and latency.

## Similarity Metrics

The similarity metric defines what "near" means in the vector space.

**Cosine similarity** measures the angle between vectors, ignoring magnitude. Most embedding models are trained with cosine objectives, making it the default choice. Range: -1 to 1 (1 = identical direction).

**Dot product** is cosine similarity scaled by vector magnitudes. For L2-normalized vectors, dot product equals cosine similarity. Normalization is model-specific: OpenAI documents its embedding vectors as length-normalized, while another model may preserve magnitude as part of the signal. The selected model's documentation, not a general assumption about every API, determines whether its vectors are normalized.

**Euclidean (L2) distance** measures straight-line distance in vector space. For length-normalized vectors, squared L2 distance equals 2 − 2 × cosine similarity, so L2 and cosine produce identical rankings; OpenAI documents this for its normalized embeddings. For unnormalized vectors, L2 also reflects vector magnitude and can rank neighbors differently from cosine, so the metric follows the geometry the model's documentation specifies.

Cosine similarity is the safe default unless the model documentation specifies another metric.

# Pitfalls

## Distribution Shift on Internal Terminology

A model that scores well on MTEB can still fail on a specific domain. Internal acronyms or product names may be poorly represented in the training data, leaving related queries and documents far apart in vector space.

Detection: recall@k on a held-out set of domain-specific queries is compared with recall@k on generic queries. A significant gap signals distribution shift.

The repair depends on the failure. Domain adaptation can improve semantic placement, while [[Retrieval|hybrid retrieval]] lets BM25 recover exact terminology that dense retrieval misses.

## Embedding Model Swap Invalidation

Changing the embedding model — even a minor version — invalidates every stored vector. The new model produces vectors in a different geometric space. Cosine similarity between old and new vectors is meaningless.

This means re-embedding the entire corpus: for a 10M-chunk index at $0.02/1M tokens and 500 tokens/chunk average, that is ~$100 and hours of ingestion time. Keying the [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/RAG Caching|embedding cache]] by model name + version prevents serving stale vectors.
